newsitem.title: FRENCH GUIANA: France gives riot-torn Guiana control of schools.
newsitem.headline: France gives riot-torn Guiana control of schools.

text.p: France said on Wednesday it would give riot-torn French Guiana control of its own schools, after unrest sparked by high school students protesting against poor conditions.
The rioting was joined by more radical groups, some of whom favour French Guiana's independence from Paris.

"It is necessary that the problems of education in Guiana are better treated and treated in a larger perspective, a perspective of development for all of Guiana," Francois Bayrou, France's education minister told student groups.

"In modern societies administration cannot be made from distance of 2,000 km (1,200 miles) that doesn't permit rapid and precise responses to problems...That is why we have decided to establish a local rectorate in French Guiana," he said.
The creation of a local rectorate was one of the main demands of school students who went on strike for three weeks in the French overseas territory on the northeast coast of South America.
The current rectorate is located in Martinique, 2,000 km (1,200 miles) away. Students and teachers say the distance mires decision-making.
At the ministers' announcement, students broke into applause and a carnival atmosphere filled the streets of Cayenne -- a city filled with fear and suspicion for the last two weeks.
Organised gangs of armed rioters fought police, looted stores and set them on fire for four nights.
The disturbances caused one death, at least 20 injuries and millions of dollars' worth of damage to property -- mostly government buildings and shops.

Pierre Dartout, the French prefect (administrator) in Guiana, described the riots as "planned actions by organised groups who aim to destabilise Guiana". He said many of the rioters were foreign nationals.
Paris sent more than 500 paramilitary riot police to patrol the streets of this city of 35,000 in case of fresh violence.

French Guiana has been in French hands since the 17th century but lags behind mainland France in housing, education and health. Official unemployment exceeds 23 percent and young people under 25, who make up 50 percent of the population, are the hardest hit.
Bayrou said he would attempt to correct the problem over the next two years of over 3,000 school age children not attending school because of lack of funds, infrastructure and teachers.
An estimated 45,000 children and young people are in school -- about one-third of the entire population.
Illegal immigrants, mostly from Haiti, Brazil and neighbouring Surinam represent an estimated 25 percent of the population of 150,000.

The immigrants were lured to French Guiana during better economic times in the late 1980s and early 1990s, triggered in part by construction at the European Space Agency launch site in Kourou and public works projects.
